title: Columns of a Tree, Top to Bottom
statement:
Place a binary tree on a grid. The root sits at row 0, column 0. A node at (row, col) has its left child at (row + 1, col − 1) and its right child at (row + 1, col + 1).

Return the values column by column, from the leftmost column to the rightmost. Inside one column, list nodes from the top row down. If two nodes share both the same row and the same column, list the smaller value first.

examples.why: 3 (right child of 2) and 5 (left child of 6) both land on row 2, column 0, under the root.
6 and 5 share row 2 and column 0. Left-to-right order would put 6 first, but the tie is broken by value.
1 is 8's right child: back in column 0, two rows below 9. Row decides before value, so 9 comes before the smaller 1.

hints: First record where every node sits: its column and row. Any traversal works for that, as long as you carry the coordinates along.
Now the output order is just a sort: by column, then row, then value.
Collect (col, row, value) triples, sort them, and start a new output group every time the column changes.

explain.intuition:
The tricky part is the tie rule. A plain BFS visits nodes level by level, left to right, which gets rows right but not ties: two different subtrees can drop nodes on the exact same spot, and then the smaller value must come first even if it was visited later.

So separate the two jobs. A traversal only records coordinates for each node. Then one sort by (col, row, value) puts everything in final order, and grouping by column produces the lists. Sorting all n triples costs O(n log n), which is the whole bill.
steps: Traverse the tree (DFS or BFS), carrying row and col. For each node push [col, row, val].
Sort the triples by column, then row, then value.
Walk the sorted list. Start a new group whenever the column differs from the previous triple's column; append the value to the current group.
pitfalls: Relying on BFS order for nodes in the same row and column. The second example breaks it.
Sorting a column by value only. Row order wins: in [9, 8, null, null, 1], 9 is above 1 and comes first.
Using a column map without tracking the smallest column, then iterating keys in insertion order instead of column order.

solutions.title: Record coordinates, sort once
solutions.idea: DFS collects (col, row, value) for every node. Sorting the triples gives the final order; group by column.

solutions.title: BFS by rows, sort only the ties
solutions.idea: BFS gives rows in order. Within one row, group the values by column and sort each small group before appending it to its column.

followups: Drop the tie rule: nodes on the same spot keep left-to-right order. Which solution becomes simpler, and can you avoid sorting entirely?
Return only the top node of each column, the view from above.
